shopping-01.rule: In a question that starts with a question word, the verb comes second: waar + kan + ik. The modal kan is conjugated, and the second verb (vinden) stays in the infinitive at the end.

examples.dutch: Waar kan ik de kaas vinden?
examples.english: Where can I find the cheese?

examples.dutch: Waar kan ik een winkelmandje krijgen?
examples.english: Where can I get a shopping basket?

examples.dutch: Waar kunnen we het brood vinden?
examples.english: Where can we find the bread?

shopping-02.rule: Ik wil graag + noun is a polite way to ask for something: graag softens the request. Alstublieft (or alsjeblieft with friends) makes it even more polite.

examples.dutch: Wij willen graag twee tickets, alstublieft.
examples.english: We would like two tickets, please.

shopping-03.rule: In a yes/no question the conjugated verb comes first: kan + ik. The second verb (betalen) goes to the end. Met de kaart means by card: met + de + noun.

examples.dutch: Kan ik met mijn telefoon betalen?
examples.english: Can I pay with my phone?

shopping-04.rule: Hoeveel kost ...? asks for a price. Tas is a de-word, so the demonstrative is deze (this). For het-words use dit.

examples.english: How much does this coat cost?
How much do these shoes cost?

shopping-05.rule: U is the polite form of you and takes the same verb form as hij/zij: heeft u. A comparative adjective before a de-word gets -e: een kleinere maat (kleiner + e).

examples.dutch: Heeft u dit ook in het blauw?
examples.english: Do you also have this in blue?

examples.dutch: Heb je ook een goedkopere tas?
examples.english: Do you also have a cheaper bag?

shopping-06.rule: Geen replaces een and means no or not any: ik heb geen zak. Use niet to negate a verb, adjective or definite noun, and geen for indefinite nouns. Nodig hebben means to need.

examples.english: I do not need a card.

shopping-07.rule: Mag ik ...? is a short polite request that means May I have ...? The verb mag comes first in the question and ik follows it. If you add another verb, it goes to the end: Mag ik even betalen?

examples.english: May I have the bill, please?

shopping-08.rule: Plural nouns always take deze (these), whether they are de- or het-words. The verb agrees with the plural subject: de appels zijn. Goedkoper is the comparative of goedkoop (cheap).

shopping-09.rule: Zoeken means to look for. Voor introduces the person the thing is meant for. Mijn does not change before de- or het-words: mijn vriendin, mijn huis.

examples.dutch: Ik zoek een cadeau voor mijn zus.
examples.english: I am looking for a gift for my sister.

examples.dutch: Ik zoek een boek voor mijn vader.
examples.english: I am looking for a book for my father.

examples.dutch: Hij zoekt een jas voor zijn zoon.
examples.english: He is looking for a coat for his son.

shopping-10.rule: Deze can stand alone as a pronoun when the noun is a de-word or plural and is already clear: ik neem deze. For a het-word, use dit: ik neem dit. The verb nemen is in second position.

examples.english: I will take these two, please.
We will take that one, thank you.

school-01.rule: Kunt u is the polite you-form: u kunt. The conjugated verb comes first in the question, and uitleggen stays in the infinitive at the end. Nog eens means once more.

examples.dutch: Kunt u het nog eens zeggen?
examples.english: Can you say it once more?

school-02.rule: Begrijpen means to understand. Niet comes after the object and negates the sentence: ik begrijp deze vraag niet. Vraag is a de-word, so deze is used.

examples.english: I do not understand the lesson.

school-03.rule: Wat betekent ...? asks for a meaning. Woord is a het-word, so you use dit and not deze. The verb betekenen agrees with the singular subject: het woord betekent.

school-04.rule: Mag ik even ...? is a polite way to ask permission. Even softens it, like a moment in English. The action verb (vragen) goes to the end.

examples.english: May I come in for a moment?

examples.dutch: Mag ik even naar het toilet?
examples.english: May I go to the toilet for a moment?

school-05.rule: The perfect tense is hebben + past participle: ik heb gemaakt. The participle goes to the end. Al means already, and mijn means my.

examples.dutch: Ik heb mijn les al geleerd.
examples.english: I have already learned my lesson.

examples.dutch: Ze heeft haar boek al gelezen.
examples.english: She has already read her book.

school-06.rule: Moeten is a modal verb, so it is conjugated (moeten with we) and the action verb stays in the infinitive at the end. Inleveren means to hand in. In questions, wanneer comes first and the verb second.

examples.english: When do we have to start?
When do I have to come?
When do they have to hand it in?

school-07.rule: Dutch often uses a position verb like liggen (to lie), staan (to stand) or zitten (to sit) instead of just to be. A pen lies (ligt), a bottle stands (staat).

examples.dutch: Mijn boek ligt op de stoel.
examples.english: My book is lying on the chair.
The bottle is on the table.

examples.dutch: Je telefoon ligt in de keuken.
examples.english: Your phone is in the kitchen.

school-08.rule: Dutch main clauses keep the verb in second position. When a time word like morgen comes first, the verb moves ahead of the subject: Morgen ga ik, not Morgen ik ga.

examples.dutch: Morgen ga ik naar de winkel.
examples.english: Tomorrow I am going to the shop.
Tonight I am going to cook.

school-09.rule: After omdat (because) the clause is a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end: omdat mijn trein vertraging heeft. In a main clause the verb stays second.

examples.dutch: Ik ben thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
examples.english: I am at home because I am ill.

examples.dutch: Hij is moe omdat hij laat gewerkt heeft.
examples.english: He is tired because he worked late.

examples.dutch: Ik ben te laat omdat de bus niet kwam.
examples.english: I am late because the bus did not come.

school-10.rule: Kunnen we ...? is a yes/no question: the verb comes first. We takes the plural form kunnen. The action verb (oefenen) is an infinitive at the end.

transport-01.rule: Van welk ... vertrekt ...? asks which platform or stop. Welk goes with het-words (het spoor), welke with de-words. Vertrekken is a regular verb and the verb comes before the subject after the question phrase.

examples.dutch: Van welk perron vertrekt de trein?
examples.english: From which platform does the train leave?

examples.dutch: Van welke halte vertrekt de bus?
examples.english: From which stop does the bus leave?
From which station are you leaving?

transport-02.rule: In a yes/no question the conjugated verb comes first: moet ik. Overstappen means to change trains. The infinitive stays together at the end after a modal verb.

examples.english: Do I have to get off here?
Do I have to change in Ghent?
Do we have to wait here?

transport-03.rule: The question starts with the verb: gaat deze trein. Trein is a de-word, so you say deze trein. Naar is used before a place name to say where something is going.

examples.dutch: Gaat deze bus naar het station?
examples.english: Does this bus go to the station?

examples.dutch: Gaat deze tram naar het centrum?
examples.english: Does this tram go to the centre?
Does this plane go to Paris?

transport-04.rule: Ik wil + een + noun + naar + place is a polite order. Naar marks the destination. Alstublieft at the end makes it polite.

examples.dutch: Ik wil twee kaartjes naar Brugge.
examples.english: I would like two tickets to Bruges.

examples.dutch: Wij willen een treinkaart naar Antwerpen.
examples.english: We would like a train ticket to Antwerp.

transport-05.rule: Aankomen is a separable verb: in a main clause it splits into komt ... aan. The prefix aan goes to the end. Hoe laat asks for the time.

examples.english: What time does the train leave?

transport-06.rule: Plaats is a de-word, so deze plaats. After zijn (is), an adjective such as vrij has no -e ending. Is starts the question because it is a yes/no question.

transport-07.rule: Vertraging hebben means to be delayed. The amount of time comes before vertraging. Mijn stays the same before de-words and het-words.

examples.dutch: Mijn bus heeft vijf minuten vertraging.
examples.english: My bus is five minutes late.

examples.dutch: De trein heeft twintig minuten vertraging.
examples.english: The train is twenty minutes late.

examples.dutch: Ons vliegtuig heeft een uur vertraging.
examples.english: Our plane is an hour late.

transport-08.rule: Waar kan ik ...? asks where you can do something. Kan stands in second position, and the action verb (kopen) goes to the end. Mijn ticket is the object in the middle.

examples.dutch: Waar kan ik een kaartje kopen?
examples.english: Where can I buy a ticket?

examples.dutch: Waar kan ik mijn fiets laten staan?
examples.english: Where can I leave my bike?

transport-09.rule: Uitstappen is separable: ik stap ... uit. The prefix uit goes to the end of the clause. Bij de volgende halte tells where and comes in the middle.

examples.english: We are getting off in Ghent.

examples.dutch: Ik stap bij het station in.
examples.english: I get on at the station.

transport-10.rule: Mij is the object form of ik (me), used after a verb: helpen mij. Mijn is possessive (my). Helpen met means to help with.

examples.dutch: Kunt u mij helpen met dit formulier?
examples.english: Can you help me with this form?

examples.dutch: Kunt u mij de weg wijzen?
examples.english: Can you show me the way?

examples.dutch: Kun je me helpen met mijn huiswerk?
examples.english: Can you help me with my homework?

home-01.rule: Sleutels is plural, so the verb is zijn (are). Mijn stays the same before plural nouns. Waar introduces the question and the verb comes second.

home-02.rule: Aan het + infinitive with zijn describes something you are doing right now: ik ben aan het koken. It is a common way to say I am cooking.

home-03.rule: The perfect tense uses hebben + participle. In a question the verb comes first: heb je. De deur op slot doen means to lock the door. Gedaan is the participle of doen.

examples.english: Did you turn off the light?

home-04.rule: The perfect tense is heb + participle (gedaan). Al means already and comes before the participle. De afwas doen means to do the dishes.

examples.dutch: Wij hebben de boodschappen al gedaan.
examples.english: We have already done the shopping.

home-05.rule: With je after the verb, the -t drops: kun je. Kun je is informal, and kunt u is polite. Openmaken is an infinitive and stays at the end after a modal.

examples.english: Can you turn on the light?
Can you help me for a moment?

home-06.rule: Dit points to a het-word or to something in general. Kopje is a het-word. Jouw means your and is informal (u uses uw). It does not change before nouns.

home-07.rule: Time phrases like na het werk can come first. The verb must then stay second, so it comes before the subject: Na het werk fiets ik. Naar huis means home.

examples.dutch: Na de les ga ik naar huis.
examples.english: After the lesson I go home.
After dinner I go for a walk.

home-08.rule: Er staat means there is, and it describes something standing or placed somewhere. Staan, liggen and zitten are position verbs and are used a lot in Dutch.

examples.dutch: Er staat een fles op tafel.
examples.english: There is a bottle on the table.

examples.dutch: Er ligt een boek op de bank.
examples.english: There is a book on the couch.

examples.dutch: Er staat een stoel in de hoek.
examples.english: There is a chair in the corner.

home-09.rule: Opruimen is separable: ik ruim ... op. The prefix op goes to the end. With a modal or in the infinitive the verb stays together: ik moet opruimen.

examples.english: We have to tidy the kitchen.

home-10.rule: Zullen we + infinitive makes a suggestion, like shall we. The infinitive goes to the end. Samen means together.

examples.english: Shall we go for a walk?

conversation-01.rule: Een beetje means a little. Spreken is a regular verb: ik spreek, jij spreekt, hij spreekt. Nederlands is a language and has no article here.

conversation-02.rule: Wat before a comparative softens it: wat langzamer means a bit more slowly. Langzamer is the comparative of langzaam (slow). Spreken stays an infinitive at the end after kun je.

examples.english: Can you speak a bit louder?
Can you talk a bit calmer?
Can you come a bit faster?

conversation-03.rule: Hoe gaat het met ...? is a fixed expression for how someone is doing. After met you use the object form: met je, met hem, met u.

examples.dutch: Hoe gaat het met je zus?

conversation-04.rule: Wonen is regular: ik woon. In marks a place where you are: in Roeselare, in Gent. Use in with cities and countries.

conversation-05.rule: Waar ... vandaan asks where someone comes from. The question word waar comes first and vandaan goes to the end. With je after the verb, the -t drops: kom je.

conversation-06.rule: Heb je ...? is a yes/no question: the verb comes first. The -t of hebt drops before je. Tijd hebben means to have time, and morgen can come in the middle.

examples.dutch: Heb je zin om te gaan?

conversation-07.rule: Ik kan + infinitive says what you can or cannot do. Niet comes before the infinitive at the end. Vandaag is a time word and sits in the middle.

conversation-08.rule: Zullen we ...? suggests an action. Om drie uur gives a clock time with om. Afspreken means to arrange to meet, and the infinitive stays at the end.

examples.dutch: Zullen we om vijf uur afspreken?
examples.english: Shall we meet at five o'clock?

examples.dutch: Zullen we om acht uur eten?
examples.english: Shall we eat at eight o'clock?

conversation-09.rule: Maar (but) joins two main clauses without changing the word order. Each clause keeps its own verb in second position. Zich voelen is reflexive: ik voel me.

examples.dutch: Ik ben blij, maar ik ben ook moe.
examples.english: I am happy, but I am also tired.

examples.dutch: Ik voel me goed, maar ik heb honger.
examples.english: I feel good, but I am hungry.

examples.dutch: Zij is ziek, maar ze werkt.
examples.english: She is ill, but she works.

conversation-10.rule: Bedankt voor + noun thanks someone for something. Voor links the thanks to the reason. Je means your before a noun (je hulp).

conversation-11.rule: Zich zorgen maken over means to worry about. The reflexive pronoun matches the subject: ik maak me, je maakt je, hij maakt zich, wij maken ons. Het verliezen is the infinitive used as a noun (losing).

examples.dutch: Ik maak me zorgen over het examen.
examples.english: I am worried about the exam.

examples.dutch: Zij maakt zich zorgen over haar zoon.
examples.english: She is worried about her son.

examples.dutch: Wij maken ons zorgen over de toekomst.
examples.english: We are worried about the future.

administration-01.rule: A question with wat starts with the question word and then the verb: wat is. De wisselkoers is a de-word, and huidig takes -e before it: de huidige wisselkoers.

shopping-11.rule: Betalen met means to pay with. Mijn does not change before a de-word. A main clause keeps the verb in second position: ik betaal met mijn creditcard.

weather-01.rule: With het as the subject, Dutch uses het is + adjective to describe the weather. After zijn the adjective has no -e: het is mistig. Erg means very.

food-01.rule: Had + participle is the past perfect: it describes something done before another past moment. Al means already. Gebakken is the participle of bakken.

examples.dutch: Ik had de soep al gekookt.
examples.english: I had already cooked the soup.

examples.dutch: Zij had de taart al gebakken.
examples.english: She had already baked the cake.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden het eten al klaar.
examples.english: We already had the food ready.

work-01.rule: Present tense for an action happening now or planned. The verb stays second: ik controleer. In the perfect, controleren has the participle gecontroleerd.

health-01.rule: An infinitive can be the subject of a sentence: rusten is goed. English uses an -ing form (resting). The verb is is singular. Goed voor means good for.

conversation-12.rule: Uw is the polite possessive (your) and goes with u. A question with wat has the verb second: wat is uw mening. Hierover means about this.

examples.english: What is your plan for this?

conversation-13.rule: The simple past of gaan is ging. Heen goes with the direction question: waar ... heen asks where to. The question word comes first, then the verb, then the subject.

work-02.rule: Zal is a modal for the future: ik zal. The second verb (opstellen) goes to the end in the infinitive. Een rapport is the object in the middle.

home-11.rule: In the simple past of zijn, ik was, wij waren, ze waren. Op zoek naar means looking for. Naar is followed by what you are looking for.

examples.dutch: Ik was op zoek naar een appartement.
examples.english: I was looking for an apartment.

examples.dutch: Wij waren op zoek naar een nieuw huis.
examples.english: We were looking for a new house.

examples.dutch: Hij was op zoek naar zijn sleutels.
examples.english: He was looking for his keys.

work-03.rule: The simple past of a regular verb adds -de or -te: eindigen becomes eindigde. The ending is the same for ik, hij and ze. Use -den/-ten for plurals.

conversation-14.rule: The perfect tense is hebben + participle: we hebben gepraat. Urenlang means for hours and goes in the middle. Gepraat is the participle of praten.

examples.english: We walked for a long time.

work-04.rule: Op de hoogte houden means to keep informed. Ik houd or ik hou are both correct. U is the polite you and is the direct object.

examples.dutch: Ik houd u op de hoogte van de planning.
examples.english: I will keep you informed of the schedule.

examples.dutch: Wij houden je op de hoogte.
Ik hou haar op de hoogte.

conversation-15.rule: In Dutch, half zes means half an hour before six, that is 5:30. English says half past five. So half zeven is 6:30 and half acht is 7:30.

examples.english: We eat at half past six.

weather-02.rule: Houden van means to love or to like. Zonnige is an adjective with -e because it stands before a plural noun. Dagen is the plural of dag.

work-05.rule: Klaar zijn met means to be finished with. Het lezen is an infinitive used as a noun. Van het rapport shows what was read.

examples.dutch: Zij is klaar met het schrijven van de brief.
examples.english: She is finished writing the letter.

examples.dutch: Ik ben klaar met het werk.
examples.english: I am finished with the work.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn klaar met het eten.

conversation-16.rule: Zul je is the future with a modal: zult drops the -t before je. Hulp nodig hebben means to need help. The infinitive hebben stays at the end.

conversation-17.rule: Zin hebben om te + infinitive means to feel like doing something. The part with om te comes at the end. Blijven is the infinitive after te.

examples.dutch: We hebben zin om te dansen.
Ik heb zin om te wandelen.
Ze heeft zin om te koken.

shopping-12.rule: The simple past of kopen is kocht (irregular). The verb is in second position. Een souvenir is a het-word.

weather-03.rule: Zullen is the future: wij zullen. Het weer controleren is the infinitive phrase at the end. Het weer is a het-word and means the weather.

conversation-18.rule: Vergeten uses zijn in the perfect: ik ben vergeten. Je naam is the object and comes before the participle.

transport-11.rule: Te lopen means that something can be reached on foot. Het is te lopen asks whether walking is possible. It differs from ver lopen, which asks about distance.

examples.english: Is the centre within walking distance?

food-02.rule: Mag ik wat ...? means may I have some. Wat in front of a noun means some. Water is a het-word and has no plural here.

examples.english: May I have some milk, please?

work-06.rule: Terugkomen op means to come back to a topic. In a main clause it splits: ik kom terug. With er + op it becomes erop: ik kom erop terug.

examples.dutch: Ik kom er later op terug.
examples.english: I will come back to it later.

examples.dutch: Wij komen daar morgen op terug.
examples.english: We will get back to that tomorrow.
She will come back to it.

food-03.rule: The perfect with drinken is hebben + gedronken. Wij hebben takes the plural form. The participle goes to the end.

transport-12.rule: Vertrekken uses zijn in the perfect: hij is vertrokken. Verbs of movement and change of place often take zijn. Geleden follows the time expression: een uur geleden means an hour ago.

examples.dutch: Zij is twee uur geleden aangekomen.

home-12.rule: Liever is the comparative of graag and means would rather. The verb stays second, and liever comes after the subject. Thuis means at home.

examples.english: We would rather eat at home.

work-07.rule: Schoonmaken is separable: maakte ... schoon in the simple past. The particle schoon goes to the end of the main clause. Het bureau is a het-word.

conversation-19.rule: The simple past of klinken is klonk (irregular). Enigszins means somewhat. An adjective after the verb has no -e: vreemd.

health-02.rule: Nodig hebben means to need. The object comes between hebben and nodig: ik heb een dokter nodig. Use it for people and things.

conversation-20.rule: In a subordinate clause with als, the conjugated verb goes to the end: als je iets nodig hebt. The main clause has the normal word order. Laat het me weten means let me know.

examples.dutch: Bel me als je hulp nodig hebt.
examples.english: Call me if you need help.

examples.dutch: Laat het weten als je komt.
examples.english: Let me know if you come.

examples.dutch: Zeg het als je moe bent.
examples.english: Say it if you are tired.

leisure-01.rule: The perfect uses hebben + participle: ze hebben gezien. Zien has the irregular participle gezien. The participle goes to the end.

work-08.rule: Bevestigen is regular in the present: ik bevestig, hij bevestigt. The participle has no ge-: bevestigd. In a main clause the verb stays second.

work-09.rule: Bezig zijn met means to be busy with. Het schrijven is an infinitive used as a noun. Druk means busy and is used here as an adverb with bezig.

examples.dutch: Hij is druk bezig met het koken.
Ik ben bezig met mijn huiswerk.
examples.english: I am busy with my homework.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn druk bezig met het project.
examples.english: We are busy with the project.

conversation-21.rule: Het eens zijn met means to agree with. The pronoun het stays fixed. Daarmee refers to the thing you agree with.

leisure-02.rule: Vroeger means in the past or used to. The simple past ging describes a habit. The verb stays second after the subject.

examples.dutch: Wij gingen vroeger naar het zwembad.
examples.english: We used to go to the pool.
She used to live in Ghent.

transport-13.rule: The simple past of vertrekken is vertrok in the singular and vertrokken in the plural. Vroeg is an adverb here and does not change.

examples.dutch: De trein vertrok om vijf uur.
examples.english: The train left at five o'clock.

conversation-22.rule: After zijn, a noun phrase with een needs the right adjective ending: with a het-word the adjective has no -e (een geweldig idee), with a de-word it does (een geweldige oplossing). Idee is a het-word.

conversation-23.rule: Waard zijn means to be worth. Het proberen waard is a set expression: it is worth trying. Het proberen is an infinitive used as a noun.

examples.dutch: Dit boek is het lezen waard.

work-10.rule: Kunnen we is a yes/no question, so the verb comes first. Samenwerken stays an infinitive at the end. Hieraan combines hier and aan: on this.

leisure-03.rule: Hun means their before a noun. Oefenen is regular: zij oefenen. The noun tekenvaardigheid is a long compound and is a de-word.

conversation-24.rule: Jou is the stressed object form of je (you). The simple past of bellen is belde. Zij belde jou is stronger than zij belde je because jou is emphasised.

conversation-25.rule: Ontmoeten has no ge- in the participle because it starts with ont-: ontmoet. The perfect uses hebben. Nieuwe takes -e before plural mensen.

weather-04.rule: Gaan + infinitive can express what is about to happen. Het gaat regenen means it is going to rain. The infinitive regenen stays at the end.

examples.english: It is going to be windy.

home-13.rule: Verantwoordelijk zijn voor means to be responsible for. The preposition voor stays with the adjective. Het opruimen is an infinitive used as a noun.

examples.dutch: Zij is verantwoordelijk voor de kinderen.
examples.english: She is responsible for the children.

examples.dutch: Ik ben verantwoordelijk voor het eten.
examples.english: I am responsible for the food.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn verantwoordelijk voor de planning.
examples.english: We are responsible for the schedule.

food-04.rule: The simple past of drinken is dronk (singular) and dronken (plural). The object follows the verb. Een limonade is a de-word.

conversation-26.rule: Aan jou denken is the subject of the sentence, an infinitive phrase. The verb doet is singular. Me glimlachen is an object and an infinitive: makes me smile.

examples.dutch: Naar muziek luisteren doet me goed.
examples.english: Listening to music does me good.

home-14.rule: Moeten is a modal verb: ik moet. Mijn telefoon is the object and the infinitive opladen goes to the end. Opladen has the stress on the first part.

examples.english: She needs to repair her bike.
We have to wash the car.

school-11.rule: Totdat introduces a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: totdat je het snapt. The imperative blijf starts the sentence without a subject. Proberen is an infinitive.

examples.english: Keep waiting until I come back.

examples.dutch: Wacht tot je naam wordt geroepen.
examples.english: Wait until your name is called.

work-11.rule: Wanneer is ...? asks about a time. The question word comes first, then the verb, then the subject. De deadline is a de-word.

work-12.rule: Laten we + infinitive makes a suggestion. Een follow-up plannen is the object and the infinitive at the end. Laten we is a fixed way to say let us.

transport-14.rule: Ver lopen asks about distance on foot. Het is ver lopen means it is a long walk. After is the adjective has no -e, and lopen is an infinitive used like a noun.

examples.dutch: Is het ver naar het station?
examples.english: Is it far to the station?

transport-15.rule: Tegenover means opposite and is a preposition. Het is + preposition + noun gives a location. Het park is a het-word.

examples.english: It is next to the station.
It is in front of the bank.

work-13.rule: Gewend zijn te + infinitive means to be used to doing something. Lange takes -e because uren is plural. The infinitive werken goes to the end after te.

examples.dutch: Ik ben gewend vroeg op te staan.
examples.english: I am used to getting up early.

examples.dutch: Zij is gewend hard te werken.
examples.english: She is used to working hard.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn gewend laat te eten.
examples.english: We are used to eating late.

school-12.rule: Uitleggen is separable: leg ... uit in the imperative. Het me means it to me. The particle uit goes to the end.

transport-16.rule: Zult u is the polite future: zullen with u. In a question with waar the verb comes second. Verblijven stays an infinitive at the end.

conversation-27.rule: Had + participle is the past perfect: it describes something that was already done earlier. Al eens means already once or before. The participle gehoord goes to the end.

examples.dutch: Ik had die film al eens gezien.
examples.english: I had already seen that film once.

examples.dutch: Zij had het al eens geprobeerd.
examples.english: She had already tried it once.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden dat liedje al eens gehoord.
examples.english: We had already heard that song once.

conversation-28.rule: In a question with a question word, the order is wat + verb + subject: wat moet ik. The modal moet is conjugated and the infinitive doen goes to the end.

examples.english: Where do I have to sign?

conversation-29.rule: Klinken is a regular verb in the present: dat klinkt. After a verb like klinken the adjective has no -e: geweldig. This is a common reaction to a plan.

food-05.rule: The perfect uses hebben + participle: heb je gegeten. In a question with waar the verb is second and the participle goes to the end. Gegeten is the participle of eten.

conversation-30.rule: Hadden + participle is the past perfect for plural subjects: we hadden gemaakt. Een keuze maken means to make a choice. Al means already.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden al een afspraak gemaakt.
examples.english: We had already made an appointment.

shopping-13.rule: After a number, units like dozijn, kilo and liter stay singular: twee dozijn, drie kilo. The thing counted follows in the plural: eieren. Het ei has the irregular plural eieren.

work-14.rule: Laten we + infinitive makes a suggestion. Laten we is followed by the object and then the infinitive at the end: laten we een deadline stellen. Nieuw takes -e before a de-word: een nieuwe deadline.

examples.dutch: Laten we een nieuwe afspraak maken.

administration-02.rule: Laat + object + infinitive means to have something done or to let it be done. Opsturen is separable, but after laat it stays whole. Naar me tells who receives it.

examples.dutch: Laat het naar mijn adres opsturen.
examples.english: Have it sent to my address.

food-06.rule: Zin hebben om te + infinitive means to feel like doing something. Ik heb zin om te eten means I feel like eating. Hebben stays conjugated.

examples.dutch: Ik heb zin om iets te drinken.
examples.english: I feel like having a drink.

examples.dutch: Heb je zin om te komen?

work-15.rule: Spreken over means to talk about. The perfect is hebben + gesproken. Over het project is the topic and comes in the middle.

examples.dutch: Wij hebben over het plan gepraat.
Zij heeft over haar werk gesproken.
Ik heb over de prijs gebeld.

transport-17.rule: Kennen means to know a person or a place. Kent u is a yes/no question with the polite u. Use weten for facts and kennen for people and places. Deze buurt: buurt is a de-word.

examples.english: Do you know a good doctor?

conversation-31.rule: Zo before an adjective means so. After zijn the adjective stays without -e: zo trots. This works like erg or heel (very).

conversation-32.rule: Aan het doen with zijn describes something happening now. The question word wat comes first, then ben je (verb before subject). The infinitive doen goes to the end.

examples.dutch: Wat ben je aan het lezen?
Wat ben je aan het koken?

leisure-04.rule: Uitkijken naar means to look forward to. It is separable: we kijken uit naar. The particle uit stays in the middle before naar.

examples.dutch: Ik kijk uit naar het weekend.
examples.english: I am looking forward to the weekend.

examples.dutch: Zij kijkt uit naar je bezoek.
examples.english: She is looking forward to your visit.

examples.dutch: Wij kijken uit naar de zomer.
examples.english: We are looking forward to the summer.

home-15.rule: Had + participle is the past perfect. Uitdoen is separable, and the participle is uitgedaan (ge- goes between the parts). Al means already.

examples.dutch: Ik had de deur al dichtgedaan.
examples.english: I had already closed the door.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden de tv al uitgedaan.
examples.english: We had already turned off the TV.

transport-18.rule: An imperative starts with the verb stem and has no subject. Here aflopen is separable: loop ... af, and the particle af goes to the end.

shopping-14.rule: Ik wil dit graag is short and polite. Wil is a modal and normally takes an infinitive, but here the verb is understood: ik wil dit hebben. Graag softens the wish.

examples.english: I would like to try that.
We would like to have this.

transport-19.rule: Er is introduces something that exists. The verb is singular for one thing and plural for many: er is wifi, er zijn stoelen. A yes/no question starts with is: is er.

food-07.rule: The simple past of a regular verb adds -de or -te: proberen becomes probeerde. Gerecht is a het-word, so een nieuw gerecht has no -e on the adjective.

food-08.rule: Mag ik ...? is a polite request. The infinitive zien goes to the end. De menukaart is a de-word and is the object.

weather-05.rule: Het is + adjective describes the weather. Hier means here. Erg is an adverb meaning very. After is the adjective has no -e.

work-16.rule: Hadden + participle is the past perfect: we hadden afgerond. Afronden is separable, and the participle is afgerond (no ge-). Vroeg is an adverb.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden het werk vroeg afgemaakt.
examples.english: We had finished the work early.

examples.dutch: Zij hadden de les vroeg beëindigd.
examples.english: They had ended the lesson early.
I had already wrapped up everything.

conversation-33.rule: Hartelijk dank is a fixed polite phrase. Hartelijk is an adverb here and does not change. You can also say hartelijk bedankt.

transport-20.rule: Waar is ...? asks for a location. The verb is second and the subject follows. Het treinstation is a het-word, so the article is het.

food-09.rule: Laten we + infinitive makes a suggestion. With gaan + drinken there are two infinitives at the end: laten we gaan drinken. Een kop koffie is a fixed measure phrase.

examples.dutch: Laten we een glas water gaan drinken.
examples.english: Let's go and have a glass of water.

conversation-34.rule: The simple past of lijken is leek (singular) and leken (plural). Lijken means to seem. After lijken the adjective has no -e.

weather-06.rule: Er was introduces something that existed in the past. The verb agrees with what follows: er was een onweersbui (singular), er waren wolken (plural).

examples.english: There was a lot of wind.

food-10.rule: The perfect uses hebben + participle. Betalen is regular, so the participle is betaald. De rekening is a de-word.

leisure-05.rule: Hoe vaak asks about frequency. After the question phrase the verb comes second: hoe vaak train je. With je after the verb, the -t drops.

examples.english: How often do you all come?

work-17.rule: Zullen is the future. In a main clause the verb stays second, so dan (then) can come in the middle. Het bespreken goes to the end in the infinitive.

leisure-06.rule: Laten we gaan + infinitive means let's go and do something. The infinitive hardlopen goes to the end. It is a common suggestion.

shopping-15.rule: Bezig zijn te + infinitive means to be busy doing something. It is a more formal version of bezig zijn met. The infinitive sluiten goes to the end.

examples.dutch: Zij is bezig het eten te maken.
examples.english: She is busy making the food.

work-18.rule: Denken over/aan + om te + infinitive means to think about doing something. Erover refers to what follows: we denken erover om te openen. Om te goes before the infinitive at the end.

examples.dutch: Wij denken erover om te verhuizen.
Zij denkt erover om te stoppen.
Ik denk erover om te leren.

shopping-16.rule: The perfect is hebben + participle. Kopen has the irregular participle gekocht. Gisteren (yesterday) is a time word and sits in the middle.

examples.dutch: Ik heb deze jas gisteren gekocht.
Wij hebben het vorige week gekocht.

conversation-35.rule: Kunnen we is a yes/no question with the verb first. Dinsdag is a day without an article. Afspreken stays at the end.

examples.english: Can we eat together on Friday?

health-03.rule: Zich voelen is reflexive: ik voelde me. The simple past voelde adds -de. Een beetje moe means a bit tired, and moe has no -e after the verb.

administration-03.rule: Ik had + participle is the past perfect. Schrijven has the irregular participle geschreven. Al means already, and de brief is a de-word.

examples.dutch: Zij had het formulier al ingevuld.
examples.english: She had already filled in the form.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden de brief al verstuurd.
examples.english: We had already sent the letter.

conversation-36.rule: Kan ik ...? asks whether you can. Je nummer is the object. The infinitive krijgen goes to the end. Je means your before a noun.

transport-21.rule: Ik zal ... wijzen is the future with zal. The indirect object (je) comes before the direct object (de weg). De weg wijzen means to show the way.

examples.dutch: Ik zal je het station wijzen.
examples.english: I will show you the station.

examples.dutch: Wij zullen u de weg tonen.
examples.english: We will show you the way.

examples.dutch: Zij zal ons het huis laten zien.
examples.english: She will show us the house.

conversation-37.rule: Terugbellen is separable: hij belt terug. After zal, the verb is the infinitive and stays together: hij zal terugbellen. This means he will call back.

transport-22.rule: Kunt u ...? is a polite request. Mij is the object form of ik. De weg wijzen means to show the way. Both kunt u and kan u are acceptable.

examples.dutch: Kunt u mij het station wijzen?
examples.english: Can you show me the station?

examples.dutch: Kunt u mij de uitgang tonen?
examples.english: Can you show me the exit?

weather-07.rule: Is het ... buiten? is a yes/no question with is first. After is the adjective has no -e: koud. Buiten means outside.

conversation-38.rule: Verzetten means to reschedule. Kunnen we is a yes/no question and the infinitive goes to the end. Dit is the object (a het-word or a general thing).

examples.dutch: Kunnen we het naar morgen verzetten?
examples.english: Can we move it to tomorrow?

conversation-39.rule: The perfect is hebben + participle. Verbergen has the irregular participle verborgen. Voor ons means from us here, and ons is the object form of wij.

examples.dutch: Zij heeft het voor ons verborgen.
Ik heb het voor jou bewaard.
examples.english: I have kept it for you.

shopping-17.rule: The simple past of dragen is droeg (irregular). Een sjaal is a de-word. The verb is second.

examples.english: I was wearing my new coat.

conversation-40.rule: The simple past of nemen is nam. Een beslissing nemen means to make a decision. Beslissing is a de-word.

home-16.rule: Leeg means empty. Mijn telefoon is leeg is used for a dead battery. Dutch often uses leeg when a battery is empty. After is the adjective has no -e.

health-04.rule: Tot introduces a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end: tot de dokter ze roept. Gaan zitten means to sit down. Ze is an object here.

examples.dutch: Ik blijf zitten tot het klaar is.
examples.english: I will keep sitting until it is done.

examples.dutch: Ze gaan staan tot de bus komt.
examples.english: They stand until the bus comes.

conversation-41.rule: Blij zijn met means to be happy about. Met introduces what makes you happy. Kans is a de-word.

examples.dutch: Hij is blij met het cadeau.
examples.english: He is happy with the gift.

examples.dutch: Zij is trots op haar werk.
examples.english: She is proud of her work.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn blij met het nieuws.
examples.english: We are happy about the news.

food-11.rule: De zak met eten means the bag of food. Met links the container to its contents. Waar is is a question with the verb second.

examples.dutch: Waar is de doos met boeken?
examples.english: Where is the box of books?

examples.dutch: Waar is de fles met water?
examples.english: Where is the bottle of water?

examples.dutch: Waar is de tas met kleren?
examples.english: Where is the bag of clothes?

conversation-42.rule: The simple past werkte is regular (werken + te). De eerste keer means the first time. Niet comes near the end.

examples.dutch: Het licht werkte de tweede keer niet.
examples.english: The light did not work the second time.

conversation-43.rule: Wazig means blurry or hazy. After zijn the adjective has no -e. Erg is an adverb meaning very.

shopping-18.rule: Heb je ...? is a yes/no question in the perfect. Voor me gives the person it is for. The participle gekocht goes to the end.

examples.dutch: Heb je het voor mij gekocht?
examples.english: Did you buy it for me?

examples.dutch: Heb je dat voor haar gemaakt?
examples.english: Did you make that for her?

examples.dutch: Heb je koffie voor ons gezet?
examples.english: Did you make coffee for us?

school-13.rule: Heel before an adjective means very. After is the adjective has no -e: heel gemakkelijk. Dit is used for something close or the thing being shown.

transport-23.rule: Op vakantie vertrekken means to leave for a holiday. Vrijdag is a day without an article. The present tense can also describe a planned future event.

examples.english: They leave on a trip tomorrow.
We go on holiday on Saturday.

school-14.rule: Voorlezen is separable: lees ... voor in the imperative. Het me means it to me. The particle voor goes to the end.

transport-24.rule: Nodig hebben means to need. The object goes between hebben and nodig: een kaart nodig. Kaart is a de-word.

leisure-07.rule: Om te + infinitive expresses a purpose: here to play. The infinitive spelen goes to the end after te. Zijn is conjugated: wij zijn.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn hier om te leren.
Ik ben hier om te helpen.
Zij zijn hier om te werken.

health-05.rule: Wassen means to wash. In the present: ik was, jij wast, hij wast. Voor elke maaltijd means before every meal. Handen is the plural of hand.

transport-25.rule: Klaar zijn om te + infinitive means to be ready to do something. Gaan stands at the end after te. Om te marks the purpose.

examples.dutch: Ik ben klaar om te beginnen.
Zij is klaar om te vertrekken.
Wij zijn klaar om te eten.

work-19.rule: Te laat means too late or late. Door het verkeer gives the reason: because of traffic. Soms means sometimes and goes after the verb.

examples.dutch: Zij is door het weer te laat.
examples.english: She is late because of the weather.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn door de drukte te laat.
examples.english: We are late because of the crowds.

home-17.rule: Wilden is the simple past plural of willen. After a modal the infinitive goes to the end: verhuizen. Groter is the comparative; with een and a het-word there is no -e: een groter huis.

examples.dutch: Ze wilden naar het buitenland verhuizen.
Hij wilde een groter huis kopen.
examples.english: He wanted to buy a bigger house.

examples.dutch: Wij wilden naar de stad verhuizen.
examples.english: We wanted to move to the city.

transport-26.rule: Waar is ...? asks where something is. Het toilet is a het-word. The verb is second and the subject follows.

health-06.rule: Worden means to become. Op een dag means one day. The present tense of worden can also express the future. After een, a de-word or het-word is fine: een geweldige dokter (dokter is a de-word, so geweldig takes -e).

examples.dutch: Hij wordt later een goede leraar.
examples.english: He will become a good teacher later.

examples.dutch: Zij wordt op een dag beroemd.
examples.english: She will become famous one day.

weather-08.rule: The simple past of zijn is was. Een prachtige zonsondergang: prachtig takes -e before a de-word with een. Zonsondergang is a de-word.

work-20.rule: The simple past plural of gebruiken is gebruikten. Voor shows the purpose. De vergaderruimte and de presentatie are de-words.

examples.dutch: Wij gebruikten de zaal voor de les.
examples.english: We used the room for the lesson.

examples.dutch: Zij gebruikte de computer voor het werk.
examples.english: She used the computer for work.

examples.dutch: Ik gebruikte het papier voor de tekening.
examples.english: I used the paper for the drawing.

work-21.rule: Uiterlijk means at the latest. Weten is irregular: ik weet, jij weet, hij weet. The present tense here refers to a future moment.

examples.english: I will know it by Friday at the latest.

examples.dutch: Wij weten het antwoord uiterlijk morgen.
examples.english: We will know the answer by tomorrow at the latest.

examples.dutch: Zij weet het resultaat uiterlijk dinsdag.
examples.english: She will know the result by Tuesday at the latest.

leisure-08.rule: Dansen met means to dance with. Present tense can describe a plan: ik dans. Op de bruiloft tells where. Je is the object after met.

examples.dutch: Ik dans met haar op het feest.
examples.english: I will dance with her at the party.

conversation-44.rule: Willen is a modal: ik wil. The infinitive sturen goes to the end. Het je sturen: het is the direct object and je the indirect object.

examples.english: I want to give it to him.

examples.dutch: Ik wil het je laten zien.
examples.english: I want to show it to you.
I want to send it to you. (polite)

conversation-45.rule: Zullen is the future: wij zullen. Je is the object after helpen. The infinitive helpen goes to the end.

conversation-46.rule: Eraan komen means to be on the way or approaching. It is separable: zij komen eraan. Er + aan combine into eraan.

conversation-47.rule: Maar can also mean only or just, not only but. Ik ben maar een gast means I am only a guest. Zijn is conjugated: ik ben, jij bent, hij is.

examples.dutch: Het is maar een kleine fout.
examples.english: It is only a small mistake.

examples.dutch: Zij is maar vijf jaar oud.
examples.english: She is only five years old.

leisure-09.rule: Komen naar means to come to a place or an event. The present tense can describe a plan. Je means your before a noun: je feestje. Feestje is a het-word.

examples.english: I will come to your birthday.
She is coming to the concert.
We are coming to your house.

home-18.rule: Vies means dirty. After het is the adjective has no -e. Erg is an adverb meaning very.

conversation-48.rule: An imperative starts with the verb stem and has no subject. Geven is irregular: geef. Het me means it to me: the thing first, then the person.

leisure-10.rule: Danste is the simple past of dansen (regular). Met introduces who you danced with. Mijn does not change before a de-word.

home-19.rule: Opblijven is separable: in the simple past it splits into bleven ... op. Vroeger means in the past and shows a habit. Laat is an adverb here.

examples.english: I used to stay up late.

weather-09.rule: Worden + adjective describes a change: it is getting cold. Het wordt koud is a common way to say the weather is changing. After worden the adjective has no -e.

home-20.rule: The simple past of wonen is woonde (singular) and woonden (plural). In de stad means in the city. The verb is second after the subject.

leisure-11.rule: The perfect is hebben + participle. Kopen has the irregular participle gekocht. De kaartjes is plural of het kaartje.

conversation-49.rule: Het is + adjective + om te + infinitive means it is difficult to do something. Om te goes with the infinitive at the end. The adjective after is has no -e.

examples.dutch: Het is makkelijk om te leren.
Het is leuk om te spelen.
Het is belangrijk om te luisteren.

conversation-50.rule: Nadenken is separable: ik denk na. Over introduces the topic. The particle na goes before over in the main clause.

examples.dutch: Ik denk na over de vraag.
examples.english: I am thinking about the question.

examples.dutch: Zij denkt na over haar toekomst.
examples.english: She is thinking about her future.

examples.dutch: Wij denken na over het plan.
examples.english: We are thinking about the plan.

weather-10.rule: Kijken naar means to look at. The simple past of kijken is keek (singular) and keken (plural). The verb is second.

administration-04.rule: A yes/no question puts the verb first. Opsturen is separable: stuur ... op. Het me means it to me; the particle op goes to the end.

examples.english: Will you send it to us?
Will you send it to me? (polite)

weather-11.rule: Helder means clear or bright. After zijn the adjective has no -e. De maan is a de-word.

work-22.rule: Ontvangen has the simple past ontving and no ge- in the participle (ontvangen). Een prijs voor means a prize for. Haar work: haar means her.

food-12.rule: Hoe is ...? asks for an opinion or description. The verb is second. Het ontbijt is a het-word.

conversation-51.rule: Had + participle is the past perfect. Zien has the irregular participle gezien. Al means already. Het nieuws is a het-word and singular.

examples.dutch: Ik had de film al gezien.
examples.english: I had already seen the film.

school-15.rule: Kunnen is a modal: ik kan. Niet comes before the infinitive at the end. Het je means it to you: the thing first, then the person.

examples.dutch: Ik kan het je niet zeggen.
Wij kunnen het hem niet laten zien.
examples.english: We cannot show it to him.

conversation-52.rule: Mijn fout means my mistake. Fout is a de-word. Het is can also point to a situation. Zijn agrees with the subject: het is.

transport-27.rule: Staan te + infinitive describes what someone is doing in a position. Ik stond te wachten means I was waiting. Bij de bushalte tells the place.

food-13.rule: In the perfect, niet comes before the participle: niet gedronken. The participle is at the end. Haar koffie is the object.

examples.dutch: Hij heeft zijn thee niet gedronken.
examples.english: He did not drink his tea.

examples.dutch: Zij hebben hun soep niet opgegeten.
examples.english: They did not finish their soup.

home-21.rule: A yes/no question puts the verb first. With je after the verb the -t drops: slaap je. Nu means now.

shopping-19.rule: Wat in front of a noun means some. The simple past of kopen is kocht. Fruit is a het-word.

work-23.rule: Praten over means to talk about. Zij praten is plural. Over de details is the topic and comes at the end.

examples.english: They are talking about the work.
We are talking about the price.
He is talking about his holiday.

transport-28.rule: Waar is ...? asks where something is. Het bed is a het-word. The verb is second and the subject follows.

conversation-53.rule: Teruggeven is separable: geef ... terug in the imperative. Het ons means it to us. The particle terug goes to the end.

transport-29.rule: Dezelfde means the same and goes with de-words and plurals. For het-words use hetzelfde. Elke keer means every time.

examples.dutch: Wij nemen elke dag dezelfde bus.
examples.english: We take the same bus every day.
I choose the same every time.

conversation-54.rule: Kunnen is a modal and the infinitive vertellen goes to the end. Nog niet means not yet. Het je means it to you.

examples.dutch: Ik kan het je nog niet zeggen.
Ik kan het nog niet doen.
Wij kunnen het nog niet begrijpen.

home-22.rule: Denken erover om te + infinitive means to think about doing something. Ze denken is plural. Verhuizen is the infinitive at the end.

examples.dutch: Wij denken erover om te vertrekken.
Hij denkt erover om te stoppen.
Ik denk erover om te beginnen.

transport-30.rule: Daarginds means over there and is an adverb of place. Het is can introduce a location. The word order is simple: het is + place.

conversation-55.rule: A yes/no question puts the verb first: spreekt u. Spreken is regular. Engels is a language without an article.

leisure-12.rule: The simple past of maken is maakte (singular) and maakten (plural). Plannen maken voor means to make plans for. Voor tells the time or purpose.

examples.dutch: Wij maakten plannen voor de zomer.
examples.english: We made plans for the summer.

school-16.rule: Moeten is a modal: je moet. The infinitive luisteren goes to the end. Je moet can also mean you have to.

leisure-13.rule: Kijken naar is used for watching something. The simple past plural is keken. De wedstrijd is a de-word.

home-23.rule: Bezig zijn met means to be busy with. Het schoonmaken is an infinitive used as a noun. Van de ramen shows the object of the cleaning.

examples.dutch: Zij is bezig met het koken van het eten.
examples.english: She is busy cooking the food.

examples.dutch: Hij is bezig met het opruimen van de tuin.
examples.english: He is busy tidying the garden.

examples.dutch: Ik ben bezig met het wassen van de kleren.
examples.english: I am busy washing the clothes.

home-24.rule: Schoon means clean. After is the adjective has no -e. Het is can describe a thing or a room.

conversation-56.rule: Wie asks who. Wie is daar nu? has the verb second. Nu means now. Daar means there.

shopping-20.rule: Dit is points to a het-word or something general. Mijn tas: tas is a de-word, mijn does not change. Zijn is conjugated: dit is.

conversation-57.rule: Vragen om te + infinitive means to ask someone to do something. The simple past plural is vroegen. Ons is the object form of wij.

examples.dutch: Ze vroeg me om te helpen.
Hij vroeg haar om te blijven.
Wij vroegen hem om te komen.

transport-31.rule: Passeren is a verb with a prefix, so it has no ge- in the participle. The simple past is passeerde (singular) and passeerden (plural). De bank is a de-word.

leisure-14.rule: In the perfect, niet comes before the participle: niet verloren. Verliezen has the irregular participle verloren. Je hebt is the second person.

examples.dutch: Hij heeft het spel niet verloren.
examples.english: He did not lose the game.

examples.dutch: Ik heb mijn sleutels niet verloren.
examples.english: I did not lose my keys.

shopping-21.rule: Contant betalen means to pay in cash. Betaalden is the simple past plural of betalen. Voor shows what you paid for.

home-25.rule: After horen you can add an object and an infinitive: ik hoor de vogels zingen. The infinitive zingen goes to the end. Elke ochtend is a time phrase.

leisure-15.rule: Beu zijn means to be tired of or fed up with. The object (deze muziek) comes before beu. Deze goes with the de-word muziek.

examples.english: I am tired of this work.
We are tired of this weather.

conversation-58.rule: Vinden means to think or to find. Ik vind zijn auto leuk means I like his car. Zijn means his before a noun. Leuk has no -e after the object.

leisure-16.rule: Ging is the simple past of gaan. Vroeger shows a habit in the past. Naar het park is a place and the verb stays second.

examples.dutch: Ik ging vroeger naar het zwembad.
examples.english: I used to go to the pool.
She used to go to school.
We used to go to the sea.

school-17.rule: Iets nieuws means something new. After iets, an adjective takes -s: iets nieuws, iets leuks, iets lekkers. Elke dag means every day.

examples.english: I want to eat something tasty.
She is looking for something beautiful.

conversation-59.rule: Gaan + infinitive expresses a plan or change. Meer means more. In zichzelf geloven means to believe in yourself; zichzelf is the reflexive form for hij, zij and ze.

examples.english: He is going to believe in himself.
I am going to believe in myself.
She is going to exercise more.

health-07.rule: Wakker worden means to wake up. The simple past of worden is werd. The sentence has two verbs joined by en: werd and voelde. Zich voelen is reflexive.

examples.dutch: Ik werd moe en ging slapen.
examples.english: I got tired and went to sleep.

conversation-60.rule: Lang means tall or long. After zijn the adjective has no -e. Erg means very.

home-26.rule: Wassen is irregular in the present: ik was, jij wast, hij wast. In de wasserette tells the place. Zijn means his before a plural noun.

examples.english: I wash my clothes at home.

leisure-17.rule: An infinitive can be the subject: bowlen is. Een leuke sociale activiteit: with een and a de-word, the adjective takes -e. Activiteit is a de-word.

conversation-61.rule: The simple past of bellen is belde. Me is the object form of ik. Vanmorgen means this morning and is a time word that can sit after the object.

conversation-62.rule: Zo terug means back soon, back in a moment. Ik ben + zo + terug is a fixed expression. Zo here means in a moment.

examples.english: I will be done in a moment.
He will be home in a moment.
We will be there in a moment.

transport-32.rule: Met de bus means by bus: met + vehicle. Naar zijn werk means to his work. Gaan is irregular: hij gaat.

examples.dutch: Zij gaat met de trein naar school.
examples.english: She goes to school by train.

examples.dutch: Ik ga met de fiets naar het werk.
examples.english: I go to work by bike.

examples.dutch: Wij gaan met de auto naar Gent.
examples.english: We go to Ghent by car.

leisure-18.rule: An infinitive can be the subject: zingen is. Haar means her before a noun. Passie is a de-word.

transport-33.rule: Weggaan is separable: we gaan ... weg. The particle weg goes to the end. Nu means now.

examples.dutch: Ik ga om vijf uur weg.

leisure-19.rule: Zijn + aan het + infinitive describes what someone is doing now. Zingen goes to the end after aan het. Nu is optional.

examples.dutch: Zij is nu aan het koken.

leisure-20.rule: An infinitive can be the subject: tekenen is. Een creatieve hobby: with een and a de-word, the adjective takes -e. Hobby is a de-word.

home-27.rule: Opmeten is separable: ik meet ... op. Het is the object and goes before the particle. The present tense can describe a plan.

conversation-63.rule: A yes/no question puts the verb first: laat je. Laten zien means to show. Het me means it to me.

examples.english: Will you show it to us?

examples.dutch: Laat je me je foto zien?
examples.english: Will you show me your photo?
Will you show it to me? (polite)

food-14.rule: Graag after a verb means like to: ze kookt graag. Voor shows who you cook for. Haar vrienden: haar means her before a plural noun.

examples.dutch: Hij werkt graag in de tuin.
examples.english: He likes to work in the garden.

conversation-64.rule: Vrij zijn om te + infinitive means to be free to do something. Je bent is the second person singular of zijn. Gaan stays at the end after te.

examples.dutch: Je bent vrij om te kiezen.
Zij is vrij om te vertrekken.
Wij zijn vrij om te komen.

food-15.rule: Zitten wachten means to sit waiting. Two infinitives can stand together at the end. The perfect is heeft + zitten wachten (not a participle). Een uur says how long.

examples.english: He waited for a long time.
She worked hard on her feet.

conversation-65.rule: The simple past of geven is gaf. Me is the indirect object, and goed advies is the direct object. Advies is a het-word, so there is no -e after goed.

work-24.rule: Waar werk je? asks where you work. The verb comes second and the subject follows: werk je (the -t drops). Werken is regular.

home-28.rule: Optillen is separable: ik til ... op. The particle op goes to the end. Het is the object and goes before op.

conversation-66.rule: Het is + comparative + om te + infinitive means it is better to do something. Beter is the comparative of goed. Helpen goes to the end after te.

examples.dutch: Het is beter om te wachten.
Het is slimmer om te vragen.
Het is veiliger om te blijven.

weather-12.rule: Wat voor ...? asks what kind of. Wat voor weer is het? asks for a description of the weather. The verb is second after the question phrase.

examples.english: What kind of food is that?
What kind of music do you hear?
What kind of day is it?

food-16.rule: Heeft iemand ...? is a yes/no question with the verb first. Iemand means someone and takes a singular verb: heeft. Water is a het-word.

school-18.rule: The perfect is hebben + participle. Uitleggen is separable, and the participle is uitgelegd. Het mij means it to me.

weather-13.rule: The simple past of kijken is keek. Kijken naar means to look at. De lucht is the sky.

shopping-22.rule: Wat is de prijs? asks for the price. The question word comes first, then the verb, then the subject. De prijs is a de-word.

conversation-67.rule: Is het ...? is a yes/no question with the verb first. After zijn the adjective has no -e: veilig. Het can mean it or the situation.

work-25.rule: Zodra introduces a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: zodra ze zich voordoen. Voordoen is separable but stays whole at the end. Zich agrees with ze.

examples.dutch: Ik bel je zodra ik aankom.
examples.english: I will call you as soon as I arrive.
We will start as soon as possible.

examples.dutch: Zij komt zodra ze klaar is.
examples.english: She comes as soon as she is ready.

conversation-68.rule: Dit is introduces a person or thing. Mijn does not change before a de-word or a het-word. Echtgenoot is the formal word for husband.

health-08.rule: Volgen means to follow. A diet is een dieet (a het-word). Gezond has no -e after een with a het-word: een gezond dieet.

leisure-21.rule: Praten over means to talk about. Zij praten is plural. De film is a de-word.

examples.english: They are talking about the book.
We are talking about the series.
He is talking about the concert.

conversation-69.rule: Als introduces a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: als mensen onbeleefd zijn. Mijn geduld verliezen means to lose patience. Zijn is plural here.

examples.dutch: Ik word boos als je te laat komt.
examples.english: I get angry when you come late.

examples.dutch: Hij wordt moe als hij lang werkt.
examples.english: He gets tired when he works long.

examples.dutch: Ik ben blij als je komt.
examples.english: I am happy when you come.

conversation-70.rule: Bang zijn voor means to be afraid of. The preposition voor stays with the adjective. De toekomst is a de-word.

examples.dutch: Ik ben bang voor de hond.
examples.english: I am afraid of the dog.

examples.dutch: Wij zijn bang voor de storm.
examples.english: We are afraid of the storm.

conversation-71.rule: Wat is het probleem? has the question word first, then the verb. Het probleem is a het-word. Zijn agrees with the subject.

transport-34.rule: Staan means to stand and shows position. Elke ochtend is a time phrase. Bij de bushalte tells where. The verb is second.

examples.dutch: Ik wacht elke dag op de bus.
examples.english: I wait for the bus every day.

examples.dutch: Zij staat elke ochtend aan het loket.
examples.english: She stands at the counter every morning.

examples.dutch: Wij zitten elke dag in de trein.
examples.english: We sit in the train every day.

work-26.rule: Gaan + infinitive expresses a plan: ze gaat vinden. Binnenkort means soon. Een nieuwe baan: baan is a de-word, so nieuw takes -e.

examples.dutch: Ik ga binnenkort een nieuwe auto kopen.
examples.english: I am going to buy a new car soon.
She is going to move soon.

examples.dutch: Wij gaan binnenkort een nieuw huis zoeken.
examples.english: We are going to look for a new house soon.

school-19.rule: The perfect of gaan uses zijn: ze is gegaan. Niet comes before the place phrase or the participle. Naar school gaan is a fixed expression.

examples.dutch: Hij is niet naar het werk gegaan.
examples.english: He did not go to work.

examples.dutch: Ik ben niet naar de les gegaan.
examples.english: I did not go to the lesson.

leisure-22.rule: Gingen is the simple past plural of gaan. Elke zomer is a time phrase. Vroeger shows a habit in the past.

examples.dutch: Wij gingen vroeger elke winter skiën.
examples.english: We used to go skiing every winter.

examples.dutch: Ze gingen vroeger elke dag zwemmen.
examples.english: They used to go swimming every day.

examples.dutch: Ik ging vroeger elke zondag naar mijn oma.
examples.english: I used to go to my grandmother every Sunday.

conversation-72.rule: Moeilijk te zeggen means hard to say. Te + infinitive after an adjective describes how hard something is. After is the adjective has no -e.

home-29.rule: Hadden + participle is the past perfect. Schoonmaken is separable, and the participle is schoongemaakt (one word). Al means already.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden de kamer al schoongemaakt.
examples.english: We had already cleaned the room.

examples.dutch: Zij had de tafel al schoongemaakt.
examples.english: She had already cleaned the table.

examples.dutch: Ik had het raam al opengemaakt.
examples.english: I had already opened the window.

conversation-73.rule: Had + participle is the past perfect. Controleren has the participle gecontroleerd. De tijd is a de-word.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden de lijst al gecontroleerd.
examples.english: We had already checked the list.

shopping-23.rule: Lijken op means to look like or resemble. Dat lijkt op goud: lijkt agrees with dat. Op is the preposition after lijken.

home-30.rule: An infinitive phrase can be the subject: de hond uitlaten is. Uitlaten is the infinitive at the end of the phrase. Taak is a de-word, so mijn taak.

examples.dutch: De tuin onderhouden is mijn taak.
examples.english: Looking after the garden is my job.

examples.dutch: De afwas doen is jouw taak.
examples.english: Doing the dishes is your job.

examples.dutch: De planten water geven is haar taak.
examples.english: Watering the plants is her job.

work-27.rule: Beginnen met means to begin with. Met de bouw van shows the subject. Volgende maand is a time phrase. Het nieuwe gebouw: nieuw takes -e after het with the definite article.

examples.dutch: Ze beginnen volgende week met het project.
examples.english: They start the project next week.

examples.dutch: Wij beginnen morgen met het werk.
Zij begint volgende maand met de cursus.
examples.english: She starts the course next month.

home-31.rule: Er een puinhoop van maken means to make a mess of it. The perfect is je hebt + participle gemaakt, and geen negates the noun puinhoop.

examples.dutch: Hij heeft er een rommeltje van gemaakt.
examples.english: He made a mess of it.

examples.dutch: Wij hebben er een feestje van gemaakt.
examples.english: We made a party of it.

examples.dutch: Ik heb er niets van gemaakt.
examples.english: I did not make anything of it.

health-09.rule: Zich voelen is reflexive: voel je je. In a question the verb comes first, and je is repeated as the reflexive pronoun. Beter is the comparative of goed.

school-20.rule: Zullen is the future. Na de training tells when. The infinitive begrijpen goes to the end. De regels is plural of de regel.

administration-05.rule: Wat is de wachttijd? asks how long the wait is. De wachttijd is a de-word. The verb is second.

examples.english: How long is the delivery time?

food-17.rule: Dorst hebben means to be thirsty. Dutch uses hebben, not zijn, for thirst and hunger. Ik heb dorst is a fixed phrase.

conversation-74.rule: The simple past of horen is hoorde. Op de radio tells the source. Het nieuws is a het-word.

examples.dutch: Wij hoorden het nieuws op tv.
examples.english: We heard the news on TV.

shopping-24.rule: Nodig hebben means to need. The object goes between hebben and nodig: mijn portemonnee nodig. De portemonnee is a de-word.

food-18.rule: The simple past plural of hebben is hadden. Geen water means no water. Geen replaces een or nothing before a noun.

home-32.rule: Ophangen is separable: ze hangen ... op. The particle op goes to the end. Vanmiddag means this afternoon and sits in the middle.

conversation-75.rule: Proberen is regular: ik probeer. Opnieuw means again. Het is the object.

transport-35.rule: Gaan + infinitive expresses a plan: ze gaat vliegen. Volgende zomer is a time phrase. Naar Londen shows the destination.

examples.dutch: Hij gaat volgende week naar Parijs reizen.
examples.english: He is going to travel to Paris next week.
We are going to fly to Spain.
I am going to drive home.

school-21.rule: Maar joins two main clauses without changing the word order. Ik wist is the simple past of weten. Vergeten uses zijn in the perfect: ik ben het vergeten.

examples.dutch: Ik wist het, maar ik zei niets.
examples.english: I knew it, but I said nothing.

examples.dutch: Zij wist het, maar ze is het vergeten.
examples.english: She knew it, but she has forgotten it.

examples.dutch: Wij wisten het, maar we waren te laat.
examples.english: We knew it, but we were too late.

work-28.rule: Schrijven is irregular in the participle but regular in the present: we schrijven. Elke week is a time phrase. Rapporten is the plural of het rapport.

examples.dutch: Zij schrijft elke maand een rapport.
examples.english: She writes a report every month.

examples.dutch: Ik schrijf elke week een brief.
examples.english: I write a letter every week.

transport-36.rule: Wanneer komen ze aan? asks when they arrive. Aankomen is separable: komen ... aan. The question word comes first and the particle aan goes to the end.

work-29.rule: Denken erover om te + infinitive means to think about doing something. Van baan veranderen means to change jobs. Veranderen goes to the end.

examples.dutch: Ik denk erover om te verhuizen.
Zij denkt erover om te stoppen.
Wij denken erover om te beginnen.

conversation-76.rule: Wat is dat voor ...? asks what kind of something is. Wat voor geluid? means what kind of noise. Voor is part of the question phrase here.

examples.english: What kind of book is that?
What kind of food is that?
What kind of place is that?

transport-37.rule: The perfect of gaan uses zijn: ze zijn gegaan. Waar ... heen asks where to. The question word comes first, then zijn, then the subject and the participle at the end.

home-33.rule: Voordat introduces a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: voordat je weggaat. Gaan + infinitive expresses a plan. Opruimen stays together at the end.

examples.dutch: Ik doe het licht uit voordat ik slaap.
examples.english: I turn off the light before I sleep.

examples.dutch: Zij ruimt op voordat ze vertrekt.
examples.english: She tidies up before she leaves.

conversation-77.rule: The simple past of lijken is leek. Ze leek means she seemed. After lijken the adjective has no -e. Verward means confused.

home-34.rule: Kweken means to grow or cultivate. Onze eigen groenten: eigen is placed after the possessive. Groenten is plural. In de tuin tells where.

shopping-25.rule: The perfect is hebben + participle. Verkopen has the irregular participle verkocht. Vorige maand means last month. Mijn oude auto: auto is a de-word, so oud takes -e.

examples.dutch: Ik heb vorige week mijn fiets verkocht.
examples.english: I sold my bike last week.

examples.dutch: Zij heeft haar oude huis verkocht.
Wij hebben onze oude bank verkocht.

conversation-78.rule: Ik wil weten waarom is a main clause with a question word at the end. Weten is irregular: ik weet. Waarom stands alone as the reason.

transport-38.rule: Te laat komen means to arrive late. The simple past plural of komen is kwamen. Ze kwamen te laat: te is part of the expression.

shopping-26.rule: Had + participle is the past perfect. De boodschappen doen means to do the shopping. Gedaan is the participle of doen.

examples.dutch: Wij hadden de boodschappen al gedaan.
examples.english: We had already done the shopping.

examples.dutch: Zij had de afwas al gedaan.
examples.english: She had already done the dishes.

examples.dutch: Ik had het werk al gedaan.
examples.english: I had already done the work.

home-35.rule: Zal is the future: ik zal. Repareren is an infinitive at the end. Voor je means for you.

examples.dutch: Ik zal het voor je maken.
examples.english: I will make it for you.

examples.dutch: Wij zullen het voor u doen.
examples.english: We will do it for you.

examples.dutch: Zij zal het voor ons repareren.
examples.english: She will repair it for us.

weather-14.rule: Eraan komen means to be approaching. De herfst is a de-word. The sentence uses komen with er + aan.

shopping-27.rule: Achter de toonbank means behind the counter. Staan shows position. In de bakkerij tells where. De toonbank is a de-word.

examples.english: She stands in front of the door.
He stands next to the till.
We are standing behind the house.

work-30.rule: Om acht uur 's ochtends means at eight in the morning. 's ochtends is a fixed phrase meaning in the mornings. Beginnen met + infinitive.

examples.dutch: Ik begin om negen uur met werken.
examples.english: I start working at nine o'clock.
She starts cooking in the morning.

examples.dutch: Wij beginnen om zeven uur met eten.
examples.english: We start eating at seven o'clock.

conversation-79.rule: Graag gedaan is a polite reply to thanks. It is a short form of ik heb dat graag gedaan. It does not change.

home-36.rule: Opmaken is separable: ik maak ... op. Mijn bed opmaken means to make my bed. Elke ochtend sits after the subject.

home-37.rule: Overgebleven is the participle of overblijven, used as an adjective: leftover. Gebruiken is regular. Voor shows the purpose. De slaapkamer is a de-word.

examples.dutch: Ze gebruiken de resterende verf voor de gang.
examples.english: They use the remaining paint for the hallway.

examples.dutch: Wij gebruiken het overgebleven brood voor soep.
examples.english: We use the leftover bread for soup.

examples.dutch: Zij gebruikt de rest voor het diner.
examples.english: She uses the rest for dinner.
